**The proposed answer 3/8 is wrong. The limit is 1/3.**

**Where the proposal goes wrong.** The solution requires only the four edge-neighbours of each hole to lie in $P$. But the boundary of a hole is a closed curve through its four corners. If a diagonal neighbour of a hole is not in $P$, that corner point lies on the boundary of the outer region (or of another hole), which violates the disjointness condition. So all eight neighbours of each hole must lie in $P$. The lattice construction then fails: every odd–odd cell $C$ is diagonal to some hole, so all of $C$ must be in $P$, giving $n = 3h$ rather than $\tfrac83 h$.

**Upper bound.** Let $H$ be the set of holes. Each hole is a single cell, since a larger bounded component uses more area for the same count. Pairwise disjoint boundaries force any two holes to have king-distance at least 2. For each hole $(x,y)$, take the $2\times 2$ block $\{x,x+1\}\times\{y,y+1\}$. It contains the hole and lies inside the $3\times 3$ block centred on it.

These $2\times 2$ blocks are pairwise disjoint: if $|x-x'|\ge 2$ or $|y-y'|\ge 2$, the blocks cannot overlap. So the union of the $3\times 3$ neighbourhoods has at least $4h$ cells. Since all of this union except the holes lies in $P$,
$$n \ge 4h - h = 3h, \qquad\text{so}\qquad h_n \le \frac{n}{3}.$$

**Lower bound (attainability).** Place holes at $(2i,2j)$ for $0\le i<m$, $0\le j<k$, and let $P$ be all remaining cells of a bounding rectangle of size about $(2m+1)\times(2k+1)$, with a one-cell border so that no hole touches the outside. Every non-hole cell is then in $P$, so $P$ is connected and the only holes are the intended ones. Its size is $n = 3mk + O(m+k)$, with $h = mk$. Hence $h_n/n \to 1/3$.

Both bounds give $\lim_{n\to\infty} h_n/n = \tfrac13$. The value $3/8$ would only follow if diagonal cells were allowed to be empty, which the stated boundary-disjointness condition rules out.

VERDICT: REJECT
